Getting Started with OECDscaleup

Source: vignettes/OECDscaleup.Rmd
OECDscaleup.Rmd
library(OECDscaleup)

Installation

The package is not on CRAN. Install it from GitHub with devtools:

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("amannj/OECDscaleup", build_vignettes = TRUE)

This installs the default branch of the repository (https://github.com/amannj/OECDscaleup); ref = "<branch or tag>" installs another version, for example ref = "stata-parity-v1_3-1" for the version that reproduces the Stata code bug for bug.

What this package does

This package builds the firm-level “high-growth firm” (HGF) / scale-up indicators used in the OECD Scale Up project, and produces the disclosure-checked aggregate tables shared back with the OECD. It translates the OECD’s original Stata packages: the “Second Package” (MASTER_OECD_p2.do and 5 worker .do files, version 1.3) and the trade package (MASTER_OECD_trade.do, version 1.0). The translation was verified table by table against the Stata code; the changelog lists every departure from the Stata code since then (bug fixes, the declared NACE revision and money unit) and why.

Firm-level microdata is confidential and never leaves the country whose national statistical institute holds it, so no real data ships with this package. Every example below uses small, fabricated data purely to demonstrate the interface — the actual numbers are meaningless. The input data are described in vignette("input-data") and vignette("input-trade-data").

The pipeline at a glance

Five pipeline functions, matching the five original .do files one-to-one:

  1. build_accounts_indicators() — cleans raw firm-level data and constructs every derived indicator (growth rates, HGF flags, categories, multi-factor productivity, …). Every other stage depends on its output.
  2. compute_characteristics() — descriptive statistics of scaler populations.
  3. compute_persistence() — growth trajectories before/after a scaling event (“transitions” and “evolutions”).
  4. compute_contribution() — job/turnover creation-vs-destruction accounting.
  5. compute_predictors() — classifies scalers by pre-period predictor quartile and regresses scaling on those predictors.

Stages 2-5 are independent of each other and only depend on stage 1’s output. All five are pure functions — data frames in, data frames out — so they can be tested and used without touching the filesystem.

run_scaleup_pipeline() performs the file I/O: it reads the raw .dta inputs, calls the five functions above in order, and writes every output as a CSV — mirroring MASTER_OECD_p2.do’s role in the original package.

The trade package works the same way: build_trade_accounts_indicators() (the panel with the firm-year trade variables merged in) and compute_trade_characteristics(), run from files by run_trade_pipeline(). check_inputs() checks the input files of both before a run.

The scaler analysis is new, not part of the Stata packages. It works on the indicators panel these pipelines write: compute_top_scalers() ranks the fastest growers among the scalers (top 50, top 1, 5, 10 and 25 %, on three growth indices), and compute_midcap_transitions() follows scalers and non-scalers into mid-cap status under three definitions (EU small mid-cap, leaving the EU SME category, 250+ employees), with exit as a competing outcome and coverage diagnostics. run_scaler_analysis() runs both from files. Every variant is written, so the choice among them is left to the analysis.

Configuration

Every stage takes a scaleup_config, built with config_scaleup(). This replaces the Stata global macros ($country, $inputdir, …) set once in MASTER_OECD_p2.do:

cfg <- config_scaleup(
  country = "FR",
  input_dir = "V:/SCALE_UP/DTA/",
  output_dir = "V:/SCALE_UP/TMP/",
  nace_revision = "2", # the NACE revision of the sector codes: "2" or "2.1"
  # nace_rev21_from = 2025, # for a panel in Rev. 2 up to 2024 and Rev. 2.1 after
  # financials_unit = "EUR", # if the money variables are in euros, not EUR thousand
  dominance = FALSE # set TRUE (with dom_vars/dom_num) if your country
  # requires dominance-rule confidentiality statistics
)

nace_revision is required: the pipeline’s sector rules are written for NACE Rev. 2, and Rev. 2.1 codes (used from reference year 2025) are converted to Rev. 2 first. The build stops if the codes do not match the declared revision, and if turnover per employee does not fit EUR thousand after financials_unit is applied.

Running the full pipeline from files

If you have base_financials_<CT>.dta (and optionally plants_RAW_<CT>.dta) prepared as described in vignette("input-data"), alongside this package’s own tl3_typology/exchange_rates reference data saved as .dta files in the same input folder (exactly as the original PDF instructions describe):

cfg <- config_scaleup(nace_revision = "2",
  country = "FR",
  input_dir = "path/to/input",
  output_dir = "path/to/output"
)
check_inputs(cfg) # errors, warnings and notes on the input files (counts only)
outputs <- run_scaleup_pipeline(cfg)

This writes n13_characteristics_FR.csv, n13_transitions_FR.csv, and so on to output_dir, plus the intermediate accounts_indicators_FR.dta back to input_dir (used for the manual confidentiality-check procedure described below). It also returns every output table as an R list, for programmatic use.

Running the pure functions directly

If you already have data loaded in R — for instance because you’re testing, or piping in data from elsewhere in an R workflow — call the five functions directly instead. Here’s a small synthetic example:

set.seed(1)
years <- 2010:2018
base_financials <- data.frame(
  idf = rep(1:20, each = length(years)),
  year = rep(years, times = 20),
  sector_1d = "C",
  sector_2d = 26,
  sector_3d = 262,
  region_2d = "FR10",
  birth_year = 2000,
  employment = as.vector(sapply(1:20, function(i) {
    pmax(10, round(stats::rlnorm(1, log(30), 0.3) * (1 + stats::rnorm(1, 0.02, 0.1))^(seq_along(years) - 1)))
  })),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
base_financials$turnover <- base_financials$employment * 100

cfg <- config_scaleup(nace_revision = "2",
  country = "FR",
  input_dir = tempdir(), # unused by the pure functions themselves
  output_dir = tempdir()
)

accounts_indicators <- build_accounts_indicators(cfg, base_financials)
characteristics <- compute_characteristics(cfg, accounts_indicators)
head(characteristics)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 20
#>    year sample category group       firm_count median_L3age median_L3employment
#>   <dbl> <chr>  <chr>    <chr>            <int>        <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1  2013 HGE10  ALL      full sample          2           10                26.5
#> 2  2014 HGE10  ALL      full sample          2           11                30.5
#> 3  2015 HGE10  ALL      full sample          2           12                34.5
#> 4  2016 HGE10  ALL      full sample          2           13                39.5
#> 5  2017 HGE10  ALL      full sample          3           14                49.3
#> 6  2018 HGE10  ALL      full sample          3           15                55.7
#> # ℹ 13 more variables: median_L3turnover <dbl>, median_employment <dbl>,
#> #   median_turnover <dbl>, median_employment_growth3y <dbl>,
#> #   median_turnover_growth3y <dbl>, median_employment_futgrowth <dbl>,
#> #   median_turnover_futgrowth <dbl>, mean_employment_growth3y <dbl>,
#> #   mean_turnover_growth3y <dbl>, mean_employment_futgrowth <dbl>,
#> #   mean_turnover_futgrowth <dbl>, share_acquisition <dbl>, L3share_young <dbl>

compute_persistence() returns a named list (transitions, evolutions_p1, evolutions_p2) since a country’s panel may be too short to produce all three; compute_predictors() similarly returns list() entirely if added_value, tangible_fixed_assets, or labour_costs aren’t present in the input data.

persistence <- compute_persistence(cfg, accounts_indicators)
names(persistence)
#> NULL

persistence has no elements here — this random 9-year panel doesn’t happen to contain a firm that scales specifically within the 2014-2016 window (transitions) or a panel reaching 2020 (evolutions), and neither is an error. Real country panels spanning more years, with genuine scaling firms, will populate one or more of transitions, evolutions_p1, evolutions_p2.

Disclosure control

Every output table can include dom_<var> dominance-concentration columns — the share of a group’s total held by its largest dom_num firms — when config$dominance is TRUE. This package’s own dominance_share() function implements that statistic and is directly usable to independently verify a value, the same way the original PDF’s confidentiality-check worked example describes doing by hand in Stata:

cfg_dom <- config_scaleup(nace_revision = "2",
  country = "FR", input_dir = tempdir(), output_dir = tempdir(),
  dominance = TRUE, dom_vars = c("employment", "turnover"), dom_num = 2
)
characteristics_dom <- compute_characteristics(cfg_dom, accounts_indicators)
characteristics_dom[1:3, c("category", "group", "sample", "dom_employment")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   category group       sample dom_employment
#>   <chr>    <chr>       <chr>           <dbl>
#> 1 ALL      full sample HGE10               1
#> 2 ALL      full sample HGE10               1
#> 3 ALL      full sample HGE10               1

Cells are not automatically blanked. As with the original Stata pipeline, the decision on which cells to suppress before sharing results externally rests with the analyst / national statistical institute — this package reports the statistics needed to make that decision, it does not make it for you.
